title: A Budget Is a Forecast You Earn Again Every Month
summary: A construction budget is not a number you set once; it is a forecast that must be rebuilt every month from what has been bought, what has changed and what is still unknown. This lesson shows how a disciplined owner structures the budget so that contingency, escalation and allowances stay visible, and how earned value tells you early whether the money and the work are moving together.
body:
The budget you approve at the start is a forecast, and its only value is how honestly it is rebuilt every month. Keep contingency, escalation and allowances on separate lines, measure money against work done, and you will see trouble while it is still small.

Recall

Q. Who owns float in a construction schedule?

A. Whoever the contract says owns it. Many contracts make float a shared project resource, available to whoever needs it first; others reserve it to the owner. If the contract is silent, the dispute is settled later and expensively.

Q. What is a work breakdown structure?

A. A hierarchy that divides the whole scope of a project into deliverable pieces, so that every piece of work, cost and schedule activity has one home and nothing is counted twice or left out.

Q. What is a currency mismatch?

A. Earning in one currency while owing in another, so that a move in the exchange rate changes what you owe without changing what you earn.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, most developers do not lose money because their first estimate was wrong. Every first estimate is wrong; that is what an estimate class tells you. They lose money because they keep reporting the first estimate long after the facts have moved, and they discover the gap at a draw meeting, in front of the lender, when the only choices left are expensive. In Week 49 Marco gave every piece of scope a home in the work breakdown structure. This week Quincy and Nadia put a price and a forecast on every one of those homes, and teach you to read the forecast before anyone else does.

The budget has layers, and each layer means something different

In plain English, a budget is several kinds of money stacked together. The professional framing separates them, because each behaves differently and belongs to a different person.

The base estimate is the priced cost of the work as currently designed: quantities multiplied by rates. Allowances are placeholder sums for items that are known to exist but not yet defined, such as a lobby finish not yet chosen. Escalation is the expected rise in prices between the date of the estimate and the date the work is bought. Contingency is money for what you do not yet know. And contingency itself has layers: design contingency, which shrinks as the drawings mature; the owner's construction contingency, held by you for changes and unforeseen conditions; and, in some contracts, a contractor's contingency inside a guaranteed price, which the contractor controls.

Here is a hypothetical example. A 20,000,000 dollar building at design development might hold a 16,000,000 dollar base estimate, 600,000 dollars of allowances, 800,000 dollars of escalation, 1,000,000 dollars of design contingency and 1,600,000 dollars of owner's construction contingency. If those five lines are merged into one, nobody can tell whether the project is healthy. If they are kept apart, you can watch design contingency fall as drawings firm up, watch escalation convert into real prices as packages are bought, and watch owner's contingency being spent only on what it was meant for.

The rule that follows is simple: escalation is not contingency, and allowances are not contingency. Escalation is a forecast of price movement, so it should be released into the cost of each package when that package is bought. Allowances should be reconciled to real prices as soon as the item is defined. Merging them into contingency makes the contingency look larger than it is.

Say that out loud now.

Escalation is a forecast of prices. Allowances are placeholders. Contingency is for what I do not know. Three lines, never one.

Bid packages turn the estimate into commitments

The budget is bought in pieces called bid packages: groups of related work, such as earthworks, concrete, curtain wall or mechanical, priced and awarded to trade contractors. Each award converts an estimated line into a committed amount. The distance between the two, positive or negative, is called buyout variance, and it is the first hard evidence of whether your estimate was right.

Applied example, hypothetical: the concrete package was estimated at 3,000,000 dollars including its share of escalation. It is awarded at 3,150,000 dollars. The buyout variance is 150,000 dollars over. The disciplined response is not to hope later packages come in under. It is to record the variance, ask why, update the forecast for every package that shares the same cause, and decide openly whether the 150,000 dollars comes from escalation not yet released, from contingency, or from a scope change elsewhere.

Earned value: is the money moving with the work?

Spending is not progress. A project can spend exactly on budget for the month and still be in trouble, because it bought less work than planned with that money. Earned value is the method that separates the two. It compares three numbers at any date. Planned value is the budgeted cost of the work scheduled to be done by now. Earned value is the budgeted cost of the work actually done by now. Actual cost is what that done work really cost.

Two ratios follow. The cost performance index is earned value divided by actual cost; below 1.0 means each dollar is buying less than a dollar of planned work. The schedule performance index is earned value divided by planned value; below 1.0 means less work is done than planned. Day 5 works this through in full. For now, hold the idea: a budget report that shows only spending against budget cannot tell you whether you are winning.

Hypothetical example: by month 6, planned value is 6,000,000 dollars, earned value 5,000,000 dollars and actual cost 5,500,000 dollars. The project has done less work than planned, and paid more than planned for what it did. Both indices are below 1.0. A simple spend report would have said 5,500,000 dollars spent against a 6,000,000 dollar plan: apparently under budget. It is not.

How the best do it

The strongest owners and cost consultants run a monthly cost report with the same columns every time: original budget, approved changes, current budget, committed cost, cost to date, forecast cost to complete, and forecast final cost, with the variance explained in words for every line that moved. They forecast final cost from the commitments and known risks, not from what is left in the budget. A small developer can copy this with one spreadsheet, one row per cost code from the work breakdown structure, and a rule that no line's forecast changes without a written reason.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: how construction costs are classified, added to the cost of the building or deducted, depends on local rules and on how the cost codes are labelled; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: a cost report you send a lender or an investor is a representation; forecasts must be honest at the date given. Banking: the lender tests balance against cost to complete, so your forecast should be the first place a shortfall appears. Governance: write down who may release contingency and up to what amount. Estate: if you are personally behind a cost-overrun guarantee, the cost report is a record your estate may one day need. Exit: the final cost sets your basis and your development spread; a buyer's diligence will rebuild it from your records.

Professional sign-off required: quantity surveyor or cost consultant, on the estimate, the escalation assumptions and the monthly forecast.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a budget reported as one blended number, so that escalation and allowances quietly prop up contingency, and the forecast is built from budget remaining rather than from commitments. The control is a layered budget with each layer on its own line, a forecast final cost built bottom up every month, and earned value alongside spending.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats a favourable buyout on one package as savings to celebrate. It is information, not profit. Until the last package is bought and the last change is settled, a saving on one line is most safely held as protection for lines not yet bought.

Callback

In Week 13, Sage taught estimate classes: an early estimate deserves a wide range and a bought-out one a narrow range. This week turns that idea into a monthly habit. Every package you buy moves part of the budget from a wide-range estimate to a narrow-range commitment, and your contingency should shrink in step. If contingency stays the same size while the design matures and packages are bought, either the estimate was badly wrong or nobody is updating it.

Recap

A budget has layers: base estimate, allowances, escalation and several kinds of contingency, each kept on its own line. Bid packages convert estimates into commitments, and buyout variance is the first hard test of the estimate. Earned value compares planned value, earned value and actual cost, so you can see whether money and work are moving together.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: Boston's Central Artery project and an estimate that did not stay honest.
checklist: My budget shows base estimate, allowances, escalation and each kind of contingency on separate lines.
I know who may release each contingency and up to what amount.
I record buyout variance for every bid package the day it is awarded.
My forecast final cost is built from commitments and known risks, not from budget remaining.
I read earned value alongside spending in every monthly report.
Every forecast change on my cost report carries a written reason.
I release escalation into a package only when that package is bought.
I have a cost consultant's signature on the escalation assumptions.
head: Field checklist
speak: A construction budget is a forecast I rebuild every month, not a number I set once. It has layers: the base estimate, which is quantities times rates; allowances, which are placeholders for items not yet defined; escalation, which is expected price movement until each package is bought; and contingency for what I do not know, split into design contingency, my own construction contingency and sometimes a contractor's contingency. Each sits on its own line, because merged together they hide the truth. The budget is bought in bid packages, and each award shows a buyout variance, the first hard test of my estimate. Spending is not progress, so I also track earned value: planned value, earned value and actual cost. If earned value divided by actual cost is below 1.0, each dollar is buying less work than planned. I build the forecast final cost from commitments and known risks, and every change to it has a written reason.
terms: Escalation allowance — a budget line for the expected rise in prices between the estimate date and the date each package of work is bought.
Buyout variance — the difference between the estimated cost of a bid package and the price at which it is actually awarded.
Earned value — the budgeted cost of the work actually completed to date, used to compare progress with planned spending and actual cost.

hostile.q: Your contingency is the same size it was at design development, but you have bought sixty percent of the packages. Why should I believe your budget?
hostile.a: That is a fair challenge, and the contingency should have moved. I will send you the cost report reconciled line by line: buyout variance on every awarded package, escalation released into those packages, allowances reconciled to real prices, and a forecast final cost built from commitments. If that shows contingency was carrying overruns it should not have, you will see the real figure and the plan to close it before the next draw.

title: Boston's Central Artery: When the Estimate Stopped Telling the Truth
summary: Boston's Central Artery and Tunnel project, built through the 1990s and 2000s, finished at several times its early estimates. Ford and Roman take the cost story through seven forensic steps, focusing on what any owner can control: how an estimate is stated, how growth is reported, and who is paid to say the forecast out loud.
body:
The Central Artery and Tunnel project in Boston did not fail because its engineering was impossible. Its cost story failed because the published estimate and the real forecast drifted apart, and for long stretches nobody with authority was paid to close the gap in public.

Recall

Q. What does total float tell you about an activity?

A. How long it can slip without delaying the project's finish date, assuming everything else goes to plan. An activity with zero total float is on the critical path.

Q. What is change control?

A. The written process by which any change to scope, cost or time is requested, priced, approved by someone with authority and recorded before the work is done.

Q. In Argentina's crisis of 2001 to 2002, what happened to contracts written in dollars?

A. Many dollar obligations inside the country were converted into pesos by government measures, so parties who thought they had a dollar contract found the currency of the contract itself had changed.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman joins me today because this is a story about the gap between a number a sponsor says and a number a sponsor knows. Lenders and investors fund the first. They lose money on the second. You will never run a public megaproject, but every project you run will have a published budget and a private forecast, and this case shows what happens when they separate.

A note on facts. The project is real and well documented: it replaced Boston's elevated Central Artery highway with tunnels and added a tunnel to the airport, with construction running from the early 1990s into the mid-2000s. Its final cost was several times the early estimates. Published figures differ depending on what is counted, financing included or not, and in which year's dollars. I deliberately use no project figures in this lesson. Where I describe how cost information moved inside the project, treat it as the general pattern reported in public reviews and press coverage, and verify specifics against those published reviews before you rely on them.

1. Timeline

The project was planned through the 1980s, approved with federal funding, and moved into heavy construction in the early 1990s. A joint venture of two large engineering firms served as management consultant to the state, responsible for design management and construction management. Over the decade, the reported estimate rose in steps. Around 2000, a large increase in the reported cost became public, and with it controversy over when the increase had been known. Major tunnels opened in stages in the early 2000s. In July 2006 a ceiling panel in a connector tunnel fell and killed a motorist, a separate failure of anchoring and inspection that is a lesson about quality, not cost.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions shaped the cost story. Stating estimates in a way that left out items, such as future inflation, that would certainly be paid. Accepting a large number of design changes and unforeseen conditions as the work went into dense, old urban ground. And reporting cost growth to funders in steps rather than as a continuous forecast, so that each increase arrived as news.

3. Assumptions

The early estimates assumed that the design was mature enough to price, that ground and utility conditions under an old city could be estimated with ordinary allowances, and that the funding authorities would accept growth if it was reported gradually. The first two assumptions were optimistic for a project of that kind. The third proved wrong when the public and the federal government lost confidence in the numbers.

4. Incentives

Every party had a rational reason to keep the headline estimate down. Sponsors needed support from funders and voters. Designers and managers working under the sponsor were not paid to make the political problem harder. Contractors bid on the scope in front of them and earned more through changes. Roman's point is that a lender would recognise this pattern immediately: when the person reporting the forecast also benefits from a low forecast, the forecast needs an independent check.

Say that out loud now.

When the person who reports the forecast benefits from a low forecast, the forecast needs someone else to check it.

5. Warning signs ignored

A steady stream of change orders on early contracts. Unforeseen conditions in the ground, which any reference class of urban tunnelling would have predicted. Estimates stated in constant dollars while the work would be paid for in future dollars. Disagreements between internal cost forecasts and published figures. Each of these is a sign that the estimate is a target rather than a forecast.

6. Point of no return

For cost, the point of no return was not one date. It was the moment the main contracts were committed and the ground was opened. After that, the question was never whether the cost would grow but how honestly the growth would be reported. The credibility damage, which drove audits, hearings and lasting distrust, came later and was optional: it came from the reporting, not from the tunnels.

7. Root cause

The root cause was that the estimate was managed as a message instead of as a forecast. An estimate that excludes certain costs, carries thin allowances for known unknowns, and is updated only when it can no longer be avoided will be wrong in only one direction. The engineering problems were real, but the owner's control system, which should have said the true number early and often, did not.

Roman's view: what this does to a lender

Imagine you lent against that budget. Your loan was sized against a total cost, and your in-balance test assumes the cost-to-complete forecast is honest. Every step increase in the reported estimate is a moment when the loan goes out of balance and the borrower must find equity. A lender who receives one surprise starts discounting every number the borrower gives afterwards: more frequent monitoring, tighter draws, higher pricing at refinance. The cost of a late forecast is not only the overrun. It is the trust premium you pay on every later deal with that lender.

The prevention

Rule 51: Report the forecast final cost, in the dollars you will actually pay, every month to the people funding the project, and never let a published estimate leave out a cost you know you will pay. Escalation, allowances for known unknowns and pending changes are part of the forecast, not footnotes to it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that your budget becomes a message you are defending rather than a forecast you are testing. The control is an independent cost review, by a cost consultant who reports to you and is not paid by the design or construction team, and a monthly forecast final cost that includes escalation and pending changes.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner holds back bad cost news until he has a solution, so that the bad news and the fix arrive together. In practice the bad news leaks first, and the delay is what destroys trust. Report the movement with your best current range, then report the fix.

Callback

In Week 2, Kema taught the outside view: before trusting your own estimate, ask how projects of this type have turned out. Urban tunnelling under an old city is a reference class with a long record of cost growth from unforeseen ground and utilities. An owner who had opened with that reference class would have carried far larger allowances, and the reported estimate would have grown less in public because it would have started closer to the truth.

Recap

A real megaproject finished at several times its early estimates. The engineering was hard, but the cost failure was in how the estimate was stated, updated and reported: costs left out, thin allowances for known unknowns, and growth announced in steps. The prevention is a forecast final cost in the dollars you will pay, reported monthly and checked independently.

Rule 51: Report the forecast final cost, in the dollars you will actually pay, every month to the people funding the project, and never let a published estimate leave out a cost you know you will pay.

Next: Nadia on The Money: how cost growth, contingency draw-down and escalation move your margin, your returns and your loan.
checklist: My published estimate includes escalation to the date each package will be bought.
My forecast final cost includes pending and likely changes, not only approved ones.
I have an independent cost consultant who reports to me, not to the design or construction team.
I compare my internal forecast with the number I have given funders every month.
I carry allowances for known unknowns sized from a reference class, not from hope.
I report cost movement with a range as soon as I know it, then report the fix.
I track change-order volume on early packages as a warning sign.
head: Field checklist
speak: Boston's Central Artery and Tunnel project replaced an elevated highway with tunnels, with construction from the early 1990s to the mid-2000s, and it finished at several times its early estimates. The engineering was hard, but the cost failure was in the owner's control system. Estimates were stated in a way that left out costs that would certainly be paid, such as future inflation. Allowances for unforeseen ground under an old city were thin. Growth was reported to funders in steps, so each increase arrived as news and trust collapsed. Every party had a reason to keep the headline number low, which is exactly when a forecast needs an independent check. For a lender, every step increase is an out-of-balance moment and a reason to distrust every number after. Rule 51: report the forecast final cost, in the dollars I will actually pay, every month, and never publish an estimate that leaves out a cost I know I will pay.
terms: Forecast final cost — the owner's current best estimate of what the whole project will cost when finished, including commitments, pending changes and remaining risk.
Constant dollars — amounts stated at one base year's prices, with future inflation removed; they understate what will actually be paid later.
Reference class — a group of similar past projects whose actual outcomes are used to test an estimate, as in the outside view.

hostile.q: You gave me a total cost at closing. Six months later it is higher, and your own team says they saw it coming. Why should I believe the new number?
hostile.a: You should not take it on trust, and I will not ask you to. The new number is a forecast final cost in the dollars we will actually pay, including escalation and pending changes, built from awarded packages and reviewed by an independent cost consultant who reports to me. I will give you the bridge from the old figure to the new one line by line, the date each item was first known, and the monthly forecast from here on, so you never hear a step change from me again.

rule: Rule 51: Report the forecast final cost, in the dollars you will actually pay, every month to the people funding the project, and never let a published estimate leave out a cost you know you will pay.

title: What a Ten Percent Overrun Really Costs the Equity
summary: A cost overrun does not reduce a developer's profit by the same percentage; because the loan is fixed, nearly all of it lands on the equity. This lesson traces a hypothetical 10 percent overrun through yield on cost, development spread, equity required and the equity multiple, and shows how escalation compounds and how contingency should be drawn down.
body:
A 10 percent overrun on total cost can cut the equity's profit by more than a third, because the loan is usually fixed at closing and the extra cost is paid almost entirely with your money. Contingency and escalation are not accounting details; they are the shock absorbers between your budget and your equity.

Recall

Q. In a schedule meeting, what is the question behind a contractor's request for more float?

A. Usually, who will pay if the job runs late. A request for float is often a request to move delay risk onto the owner without saying so.

Q. What is a schedule of values?

A. The contractor's breakdown of the contract price into lines, which each monthly payment application is billed against.

Q. What does a currency hedge cost you, even when it is never needed?

A. A premium or a forward rate that is worse than today's rate. It is the price of certainty, and it reduces returns in the cases where the currency would not have moved against you.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, in Day 2 Ford showed how an estimate that stops telling the truth destroys trust. Today I show you what it destroys in money. A developer who understands only total cost will treat a 10 percent overrun as a 10 percent problem. It is not. Because of how a development is financed, it is a much larger problem for whoever owns the equity, and you will usually be that person.

From cost to value: the spread is thin

Start with the measures Sage taught in Week 10. Yield on cost is stabilised net operating income, the income after operating expenses but before debt service, divided by total development cost. The market values the finished building by dividing the same income by the market capitalisation rate. The development spread is the gap between yield on cost and the market cap rate, and it is the developer's margin for risk.

Hypothetical example. Total development cost is 20,000,000 dollars. Stabilised net operating income is 1,400,000 dollars. Yield on cost is 1,400,000 divided by 20,000,000, which is 7.0 percent. The market cap rate is 5.5 percent, so the finished value is 1,400,000 divided by 0.055, about 25,450,000 dollars. The profit on cost is about 5,450,000 dollars.

Now add a 10 percent overrun: total cost becomes 22,000,000 dollars. Yield on cost falls to 1,400,000 divided by 22,000,000, about 6.36 percent. The spread over the 5.5 percent cap rate falls from 1.5 percentage points to about 0.86 percentage points. Value has not changed, so profit falls from about 5,450,000 dollars to about 3,450,000 dollars: a 37 percent fall in profit from a 10 percent rise in cost.

Why the equity takes almost all of it

A construction loan is usually sized at closing as a share of approved cost, called loan to cost. Lenders rarely increase it when costs rise; that is commercial practice, not a rule, and your loan documents decide. Suppose the loan is fixed at 13,000,000 dollars, 65 percent of the original 20,000,000 dollar cost. Equity was 7,000,000 dollars.

With the overrun, the loan stays at 13,000,000 dollars and equity rises to 9,000,000 dollars. The equity multiple, which is total cash back to equity divided by equity invested, was 7,000,000 plus 5,450,000, over 7,000,000: about 1.78 times. After the overrun it is 9,000,000 plus 3,450,000, over 9,000,000: about 1.38 times. The project still makes money. But the equity put in 29 percent more and earned 37 percent less, and the internal rate of return falls further because the extra equity usually goes in late, during construction, when there is no time left to earn it back.

Say that out loud now.

The loan is fixed. The overrun is mine. A 10 percent cost problem is a 37 percent profit problem.

Escalation compounds, and contingency has a shape

Escalation is calculated to the midpoint of when each package will actually be bought or built, not to the start date. Hypothetical: a 10,000,000 dollar package priced today, assumed to rise 4 percent a year, with its midpoint 18 months away. The factor is 1.04 raised to the power 1.5, about 1.0606, so the escalated cost is about 10,606,000 dollars. Pricing it at today's cost would understate it by about 606,000 dollars, and that gap is exactly the kind of known cost Rule 51 says must never be left out. The 4 percent is a hypothetical assumption; the real rate is a judgement your cost consultant must document.

Contingency should be drawn down roughly in step with risk retired. Early in construction, foundations and ground conditions carry the most unknowns, so contingency use is often heavier there. A useful monthly check is to compare the percentage of contingency spent with the percentage of work complete. If the job is 30 percent complete and 60 percent of contingency is gone, the remaining 70 percent of the work has 40 percent of the cushion, and your forecast should say so now.

The same discipline applies in reverse. When a package is bought under its estimate, the saving is not profit yet. It is most safely moved into contingency, where it protects the packages not yet bought, and released to the equity only when the last major package is committed and the remaining risk is small. A developer who spends early savings on upgrades, or reports them to investors as margin, has usually spent the cushion he will need in month 14. On the hypothetical numbers above, every 200,000 dollars kept in reserve is worth roughly 10 percent of the overrun the equity could otherwise have had to fund.

How the accountant sees it

In the owner's books, development costs are generally capitalised, meaning recorded as part of the asset rather than as expenses, while the building is under construction. That makes an overrun invisible on the income statement during construction: it simply raises the cost of the asset. The risk surfaces at completion, when the asset's carrying value is tested against what it is worth. If cost has grown past value, an accountant may require a write-down. Accounting rules differ by framework and jurisdiction; verify that against the primary source and your accountant before you rely on it.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

Warrick's point for your personal balance sheet is this. An overrun is a call on your liquidity at the worst moment: late in construction, when the project's own cash is fully committed. If your liquidity floor, the cash you never touch, from Week 7, is not sized for a cost-overrun call, you will fund it by selling something in a hurry, borrowing personally on poor terms, or giving away equity to a new partner. Before you sign a cost-overrun guarantee, ask what a 10 percent overrun would demand from you personally and where that cash would come from. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financing decision.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is underestimating how hard cost growth falls on equity, and so sizing contingency and personal liquidity for a small problem. The control is to model the equity effect of a 5, 10 and 15 percent overrun before closing, and to keep the overrun reserve where you can reach it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner escalates every package from the start date to the finish date, or not at all. Escalate each package to the midpoint of its own purchase and installation, and record the assumed rate.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman built base, downside and severe cases and tornado charts. Total development cost is almost always one of the longest bars on a development tornado chart, because a small percentage move in cost changes the equity's profit by a large percentage. Today's arithmetic is why that bar is so long.

Recap

A 10 percent overrun cut the yield on cost from 7.0 to about 6.36 percent and the equity's profit by 37 percent, because the loan was fixed and the equity paid for the overrun. Escalation compounds to each package's midpoint. Contingency should fall roughly as risk is retired, and the percentage spent should be compared with the percentage complete.

Next: LEX on The Rules: escalation clauses, contingency ownership and what a contract says about who pays for rising prices.
checklist: I have modelled the equity effect of a 5, 10 and 15 percent overrun before closing.
I know whether my loan can be increased if costs rise, and on what terms.
Each package is escalated to the midpoint of its purchase and installation.
The escalation rate is a documented assumption signed off by my cost consultant.
I compare contingency spent with work complete every month.
I know where my personal overrun cash would come from without selling in a hurry.
My accountant has told me how a cost-over-value gap would be treated at completion.
head: Field checklist
speak: Cost overruns hit the equity much harder than total cost. In a hypothetical project, cost of 20,000,000 dollars and income of 1,400,000 dollars give a 7.0 percent yield on cost, against a 5.5 percent market cap rate. Value is about 25,450,000 dollars and profit about 5,450,000. A 10 percent overrun raises cost to 22,000,000, cuts yield on cost to about 6.36 percent and profit to about 3,450,000: a 37 percent fall. The loan is usually fixed at closing, so the equity pays the whole overrun, rising from 7,000,000 to 9,000,000 dollars, and the equity multiple falls from about 1.78 to about 1.38 times. Escalation compounds to each package's midpoint, so I never price future work at today's cost. Contingency should fall as risk is retired, and I compare the share spent with the share of work complete. And I size my personal liquidity for an overrun call before I sign a guarantee.
terms: Loan to cost — the loan amount as a percentage of total approved development cost, usually set at closing.
Escalation midpoint — the point in time, roughly halfway through a package's purchase and installation, to which its prices are escalated.
Capitalised cost — a cost recorded as part of the value of an asset on the balance sheet rather than as an expense in the year it is paid.

hostile.q: You say the overrun is only 10 percent. Why is your equity investor so upset?
hostile.a: Because the loan is fixed at closing, the whole overrun falls on equity. On our hypothetical numbers, cost rose 10 percent, but equity had to put in 29 percent more and its profit fell 37 percent, with the multiple dropping from about 1.78 to about 1.38 times. The investor is right to focus on that. I will show the line-by-line cause, what remains in contingency against work remaining, and what we are doing to protect the rest of the budget.

title: Who Pays When Prices Rise: Escalation, Allowances and Contingency in the Contract
summary: Whether rising material and labour prices fall on the owner or the contractor is decided by the contract, not by fairness. This lesson covers the three common answers, fixed price, cost reimbursement and indexed adjustment, and how allowances, contingency and audit rights are written. It closes with a conceptual comparison of how Canada and Guyana approach the point.
body:
Rising prices do not by themselves change a construction contract; the contract decides who carries them. Read the price clause, the allowance clause, the contingency clause and the audit clause together, because together they answer the only question that matters when steel jumps: who pays.

Recall

Q. In the schedule week's review, what was the difference between a look-ahead and the baseline schedule?

A. The baseline is the approved plan that progress is measured against. A look-ahead is a short-range working schedule, often three to six weeks, that the field uses to plan the next work in detail.

Q. What should a change order clause require before changed work starts?

A. A written instruction from someone with authority, a priced or agreed method of pricing, and the effect on time, so that nobody can later argue the work was free or was never authorised.

Q. What does political-risk insurance typically cover?

A. Losses from defined government actions such as expropriation, currency inconvertibility or transfer restrictions, and political violence, subject to the policy's own definitions and exclusions.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Nadia showed you that an overrun lands on your equity. Today I show you where in the contract that landing is decided. You cannot negotiate the price of steel. You can negotiate who carries its movement, and you do that before signing, not after the supplier's letter arrives.

The default: a price is a price

In plain English, if you agree a fixed price and costs rise, the contractor usually absorbs it. The professional framing: in common law systems, courts generally hold parties to their bargain, and a contract does not end merely because performance became more expensive. A frequently cited English case, Davis Contractors against Fareham Urban District Council, decided by the House of Lords in 1956, held that a builder whose job took far longer and cost far more than expected because of labour shortages could not escape the fixed price by arguing the contract had been frustrated. How your own jurisdiction applies that principle is a question for your lawyer; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

The practical consequence cuts both ways. A contractor carrying price risk on a fixed price will price that risk into the bid. And if prices rise far enough, a fixed price that the contractor cannot afford to perform is a fixed price that may not be performed: the contractor may fail, slow down or look for claims elsewhere. A fixed price moves risk on paper. It does not make the risk disappear.

Three ways to allocate price movement

First, fixed or stipulated price: the contractor carries price movement, and you pay for that certainty in the bid. Second, cost reimbursement, often cost plus a fee, sometimes capped by a guaranteed maximum price: you pay actual cost, so you carry price movement up to any cap. Third, indexed adjustment, sometimes called a price adjustment or fluctuation clause: the contract price moves with a published index for named materials or labour, by an agreed formula. The international standard forms published by FIDIC, for example, include a mechanism for adjusting for changes in cost that applies only if the parties complete the indexation data; verify the current edition's wording before you rely on it.

Applied example, hypothetical. A 2,000,000 dollar structural steel package. Under a fixed price, the contractor might add a premium for price risk, say 100,000 dollars. Under an index clause, the base price is 1,900,000 dollars and moves with a named steel index, measured from the bid date to the date of purchase; if the index rises 5 percent, the owner pays 95,000 dollars more, and if it falls, the owner pays less. The choice is not which is cheaper. It is whether you want to pay a known premium for certainty, or carry a measurable risk in exchange for a lower base price.

Say that out loud now.

A fixed price moves the risk on paper. An index clause moves it by formula. Either way, I decide it before signing.

Allowances, contingency and audit rights

An allowance in a contract is a stated sum for an item not yet defined. The clause should say what the sum includes, such as material only or material plus installation, and that the contract price will be adjusted up or down to the actual cost when the item is chosen. A vague allowance becomes a dispute: the contractor says installation was extra, and you say it was included.

Contingency inside a contract is a different animal. Under a guaranteed maximum price, the contractor may hold its own contingency for its own risks, such as buyout gaps and coordination errors. The contract should say what that contingency may be used for, who approves its use, whether unused contingency returns to the owner or is shared, and how it is reported. Your owner's contingency should normally sit outside the contract entirely, in your own budget, so that the contractor cannot treat it as available money.

Audit rights let the owner inspect the contractor's books for any cost-reimbursable part of the price. Without them, cost plus a fee is cost as reported plus a fee. The clause should name the records, the period they must be kept, and what happens to overcharges found.

A related term is the shared-savings clause, common under a guaranteed maximum price. If the final cost comes in under the cap, the savings are split by an agreed percentage. The split is commercial practice, not a standard, and it changes behaviour: a contractor that keeps part of the savings has a reason to buy well, but also a reason to pad the cap at the start. Ask how the cap was built before you agree how its savings are shared.

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

Treat this as a conceptual comparison only; verify against primary source before you rely on any of it. Canada's provinces outside Quebec follow the common law of contract, and Quebec's civil code has its own rules on contract and on changed circumstances. Private Canadian projects often use the national standard forms of the Canadian Construction Documents Committee, including a widely used stipulated price form, amended by the parties. Guyana's contract law also follows the common law tradition. Public works there are governed by public procurement legislation and rules on tendering and contract award [unverified — confirm independently], and projects funded by development lenders often use the international FIDIC forms. In both countries, whether price movement is adjusted depends mainly on what the parties wrote, so the work is in the drafting.

Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer, on the price, allowance, contingency and audit clauses before signing.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is signing a fixed price in a rising market with a contractor whose margin cannot absorb the rise, and believing the risk has gone. The control is to test the contractor's capacity to carry price risk, to consider an index clause for volatile materials, and to secure a performance bond or other security where the exposure is large.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner lets the contractor's contingency and the owner's contingency sit on the same line in the contract, or lets the contract describe owner's contingency as available to the contractor. Keep your own contingency out of the contract.

Callback

In Week 20, I taught that a letter of intent may bind more than you think and a term sheet less. Price adjustment is where that lesson bites in construction: a letter of intent that says the contractor may start work at agreed rates, with the final price to be settled later, often leaves escalation open, and the first steel invoice settles it in the contractor's favour.

Recap

Rising prices generally do not end or change a contract; the contract allocates them. Fixed price moves risk to the contractor at a premium; cost reimbursement keeps it with you up to any cap; index clauses move it by formula. Allowances must say what they include, contractor contingency must have rules, and cost-plus work needs audit rights.

Next: Quincy on The Numbers: earned value worked step by step, from planned value to estimate at completion.
checklist: I know whether each package is fixed price, cost reimbursable or indexed.
Every allowance in the contract says what it includes and how it adjusts.
The contractor's contingency has written rules on use, approval, reporting and return.
My owner's contingency sits outside the contract.
Every cost-reimbursable price carries audit rights over named records.
I have tested whether the contractor can absorb price risk on a fixed price.
A construction lawyer has reviewed the price clauses before signing.
head: Field checklist
speak: Rising prices do not change a construction contract by themselves. The contract decides who pays. Courts in common law systems usually hold parties to a fixed price even when the job becomes far more expensive; the classic English example is Davis Contractors against Fareham, decided in 1956. So I choose deliberately. A fixed price puts price movement on the contractor, who prices it into the bid. Cost reimbursement keeps it with me, up to any guaranteed maximum price. An index clause moves it by formula, with a named index and dates. Allowances must say exactly what they include and how they adjust. A contractor's contingency inside a guaranteed price needs rules on use, approval and return, and my own contingency stays outside the contract. Cost-plus work needs audit rights. And I remember that a fixed price moves risk on paper; if the contractor cannot afford it, the risk comes back to me.
terms: Stipulated price — a fixed contract price for defined work, under which the contractor generally carries cost increases.
Price adjustment clause — a contract term that changes the price by an agreed formula as a published cost index moves.
Audit rights — a contract right for the owner to inspect the contractor's records supporting any cost-reimbursable charges.

hostile.q: Steel is up 20 percent and your contractor says it cannot hold the price. Your contract is fixed. Why not just enforce it?
hostile.a: I may well enforce it, and the contract is on my side. But a fixed price the contractor cannot afford is a fixed price that may not be performed. Before I decide, I want its open-book evidence of the increase, its financial position and its bond. If it is solvent and the claim is weak, it performs. If enforcement risks a failed contractor mid-structure, I will weigh a limited, documented adjustment against the cost of replacing it, and record why.

title: Earned Value, Step by Step: From Month 6 to the Final Cost
summary: A worked earned value calculation on a hypothetical 12,000,000 dollar construction budget at month 6. Step by step, with units: planned value, earned value and actual cost, the two variances, the two performance indices, three estimates at completion and the index needed to finish on budget.
body:
With three numbers, planned value, earned value and actual cost, you can tell at month 6 roughly what the project will cost at the end. On today's hypothetical numbers that is about 13,200,000 dollars against a 12,000,000 dollar budget, and the time to act is now, not at month 11.

Recall

Q. Why should escalation never be merged into contingency?

A. Because escalation is a forecast of price movement that will be paid as packages are bought, while contingency is for what you do not know. Merging them makes contingency look larger than it really is.

Q. In the scope week's numbers, what is the effect of an exclusion that nobody priced?

A. It becomes a change order later, usually at a worse price than if it had been bought with the original package, and it consumes contingency that was meant for unknowns.

Q. How do you convert a foreign-currency cost into home currency for a budget?

A. Multiply the foreign amount by the exchange rate expressed as home currency per unit of foreign currency, and record the rate and date, because the rate on the payment date may differ.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, in Day 1 I said spending is not progress. Today you prove it with arithmetic. This is the calculation a lender's monitor, a cost consultant or a sharp investor will do on your project whether you do it or not. Do it first.

Step 1: set out the three numbers

Hypothetical project: a hard-cost budget, called budget at completion, of 12,000,000 dollars over a 12-month construction programme. We are at the end of month 6.

Planned value is the budgeted cost of the work the baseline schedule said would be done by now: 5,400,000 dollars. Actual cost is what has been spent, or more precisely incurred, on the work done: 5,280,000 dollars. Earned value is the budgeted cost of the work actually done.

Earned value is measured line by line, from quantities, not from the contractor's billing. Example: concrete has a budget of 3,000,000 dollars. The design quantity is 6,000 cubic metres, and 3,600 cubic metres have been placed and accepted. Percent complete is 3,600 divided by 6,000, which is 60 percent, so earned value on concrete is 0.60 times 3,000,000, which is 1,800,000 dollars. Repeat for every line and add them up. Here the total earned value is 4,800,000 dollars.

Where a line cannot be measured in units, agree a rule in advance and stick to it. A weighted-milestone rule gives fixed shares of the budget for defined steps: for an elevator, perhaps a share for shop drawings approved, a share for delivery, a share for installation and the rest for inspection passed. A zero-or-hundred rule gives nothing until the item is complete, which is conservative and suits small items. What you must never do is let percent complete be a feeling, because a feeling is always optimistic at month 6.

MeasureValue at month 6
Budget at completion12,000,000 dollars
Planned value5,400,000 dollars
Earned value4,800,000 dollars
Actual cost5,280,000 dollars

Notice what a simple spend report would say: 5,280,000 dollars spent against a 5,400,000 dollar plan, so 120,000 dollars under budget. That reading is wrong, and the next steps show why.

Step 2: the two variances

Cost variance is earned value minus actual cost: 4,800,000 minus 5,280,000 equals minus 480,000 dollars. The work done so far cost 480,000 dollars more than its budget.

Schedule variance is earned value minus planned value: 4,800,000 minus 5,400,000 equals minus 600,000 dollars. The project has done 600,000 dollars less work than planned. Schedule variance is stated in dollars, which feels odd, but it means the value of work that should have been done and was not.

Step 3: the two indices

Cost performance index is earned value divided by actual cost: 4,800,000 divided by 5,280,000, about 0.909. Each dollar spent has bought about 91 cents of budgeted work.

Schedule performance index is earned value divided by planned value: 4,800,000 divided by 5,400,000, about 0.889. The project is doing work at about 89 percent of the planned rate.

Say that out loud now.

Earned value over actual cost is cost efficiency. Earned value over planned value is schedule efficiency. Below one is bad.

Step 4: three estimates at completion

Estimate at completion is the forecast total cost. There are several formulas, and each makes an assumption about the future, so state the assumption with the number.

Method A, the remaining work goes exactly to budget: actual cost plus budget at completion minus earned value. That is 5,280,000 plus 12,000,000 minus 4,800,000, which is 5,280,000 plus 7,200,000, equals 12,480,000 dollars. This assumes the overrun so far was a one-off. It is the most optimistic and usually the least defensible.

Method B, the remaining work continues at today's cost efficiency: budget at completion divided by the cost performance index. Exactly, 12,000,000 times 5,280,000 divided by 4,800,000 equals 13,200,000 dollars. This is the most common forecast.

Method C, cost and schedule problems compound: actual cost plus the remaining budgeted work divided by the product of the two indices. The product is about 0.909 times 0.889, about 0.808. Remaining budgeted work is 7,200,000 dollars, divided by 0.808, is about 8,910,000 dollars. Add actual cost: about 14,190,000 dollars. This is the pessimistic case, used when late work is being bought at premium prices to catch up.

Step 5: the remaining numbers and the hard question

Estimate to complete, using Method B, is 13,200,000 minus 5,280,000, equals 7,920,000 dollars still to spend. Variance at completion is budget at completion minus estimate at completion: 12,000,000 minus 13,200,000, equals minus 1,200,000 dollars, a 10 percent overrun.

Now the hard question: what efficiency would the rest of the job need to finish on the original budget? That is the to-complete performance index: remaining budgeted work divided by remaining budget money. Remaining work is 7,200,000 dollars; remaining money is 12,000,000 minus 5,280,000, which is 6,720,000 dollars. The index is 7,200,000 divided by 6,720,000, about 1.071. The team has been working at 0.909 and would have to work at 1.071 for the rest of the job. Experience across many projects is that a cost performance index rarely improves that much after the early part of a job; treat a plan that depends on it as a hope.

A rough schedule check: 12 months divided by a schedule performance index of 0.889 suggests about 13.5 months. Use it only as a flag. Schedule performance index drifts toward 1.0 at the end of every job, because all planned work is eventually earned, so the critical path from Week 50, not this index, decides the real finish date.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is computing earned value from the contractor's billing percentages. Then earned value equals whatever was billed, a front-loaded schedule of values inflates it, and every index looks better than reality. The control is to measure earned value from verified quantities and milestones on each cost line.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reports Method A because it is the smallest number. Report Method B as the forecast, show A and C as the range, and say which assumption you believe and why.

Callback

In Week 40, Priya taught the in-balance test: undisbursed loan plus equity to come must cover the cost to complete. Today's estimate to complete of 7,920,000 dollars is exactly the number that test needs. If the lender's remaining funds are sized to the original budget, a 1,200,000 dollar variance at completion is the deposit you may be asked to make, and earned value lets you see it at month 6 instead of month 11.

Recap

Planned value 5,400,000, earned value 4,800,000 and actual cost 5,280,000 dollars gave a cost variance of minus 480,000 and a schedule variance of minus 600,000 dollars, a cost index of about 0.909 and a schedule index of about 0.889. The forecast final cost is about 13,200,000 dollars, with a range of about 12,480,000 to 14,190,000, and finishing on budget would need an efficiency of about 1.071.

Next: Quincy on The Room: the monthly cost meeting where you tell the lender's monitor the forecast before he tells you.
checklist: I measure earned value from verified quantities and milestones, line by line.
I compute cost variance and schedule variance every month.
I compute the cost and schedule performance indices every month.
I report the estimate at completion with its method and assumption stated.
I show a range of estimates at completion, not one convenient number.
I compute the to-complete performance index and test whether it is believable.
I use the critical path, not the schedule index, to forecast the finish date.
head: Field checklist
speak: Earned value needs three numbers. On a hypothetical 12,000,000 dollar budget at month 6, planned value, the budgeted cost of work scheduled by now, is 5,400,000 dollars. Earned value, the budgeted cost of work actually done, measured from quantities, is 4,800,000. Actual cost is 5,280,000. A spend report would call that 120,000 dollars under budget. It is not. Cost variance is earned value minus actual cost, minus 480,000. Schedule variance is earned value minus planned value, minus 600,000. The cost index is earned value over actual cost, about 0.909, and the schedule index is earned value over planned value, about 0.889. Dividing the budget by the cost index gives an estimate at completion of 13,200,000 dollars, a 10 percent overrun, with a range from about 12,480,000 to 14,190,000. To finish on budget, the rest of the job would need an efficiency of about 1.071. That is a hope, not a plan, so I act at month 6.
terms: Planned value — the budgeted cost of the work the baseline schedule says should be complete by a given date.
Cost performance index — earned value divided by actual cost; below 1.0 means each dollar spent is buying less than a dollar of planned work.
To-complete performance index — the cost efficiency the remaining work must achieve to finish on a target budget, equal to remaining budgeted work divided by remaining money.

hostile.q: Your monthly report says you are 120,000 dollars under budget. My monitor says you are heading for a 1.2 million dollar overrun. Who is right?
hostile.a: Your monitor is right, and my report should have said so. Spending against plan looks under budget only because less work was done than planned. On earned value from verified quantities, the cost index is about 0.909 and the forecast final cost is about 13,200,000 dollars, a 1,200,000 dollar overrun. I will reissue the report on that basis, with the range and the plan to close the gap before the next draw.

title: The Cost Meeting: Say the Forecast Before the Monitor Does
summary: A realistic month-6 meeting with the lender, the lender's monitor and the contractor, where the owner must report a forecast overrun. The lesson gives the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind each question, when to stay silent and how to hold steady when the room turns cold.
body:
In a cost meeting, the person who states the bad number first owns the conversation, and the person who is caught with it loses the room. Bring the forecast, the cause, the range and the plan, in that order, and say it before anyone asks.

Recall

Q. What was the root cause of the Central Artery cost failure, as Ford framed it?

A. That the estimate was managed as a message instead of as a forecast: costs left out, thin allowances for known unknowns, and growth reported only when it could no longer be avoided.

Q. In the scope meeting, what is the right response when a contractor says an item was always excluded?

A. Ask to see the exclusion in writing in the contract documents, then decide on the record whether it is a genuine exclusion, a change or a gap in the design, rather than arguing from memory.

Q. When a lender raises currency risk in a meeting, what is the question behind the question?

A. Usually, how will you repay me if the currency you earn in falls against the currency you owe. They want to hear the hedge, the cushion and who carries the loss.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Day 5 produced a forecast of about 13,200,000 dollars against a 12,000,000 dollar budget at month 6. Numbers like that are survivable. What is not survivable is the lender learning it from its own monitor while you are still describing the project as on budget. This lesson is that meeting, rehearsed.

The scene

A meeting room near the site, hypothetical. Present: you, as owner; your cost consultant; the lender's relationship manager; the lender's monitor, an independent cost consultant who reports to the bank; and the contractor's project manager. The agenda says monthly cost and draw review. The monitor's draft report, which you have not seen, shows a cost performance index of about 0.91. Your own report, prepared the night before, shows the same.

You open, before the agenda's first item.

"Before we start, I want to give you the headline. On earned value measured from quantities, our forecast final cost is about 13,200,000 dollars against a 12,000,000 dollar budget. The range is about 12,500,000 to 14,200,000. The cause is concentrated in two places: foundations, where rock was shallower than the geotechnical report suggested, and the concrete package, which was bought above estimate. I will walk you through the bridge, what remains in contingency, and the plan. Then I would like to hear the monitor's view."

That is four sentences of substance: the number, the range, the cause and the agenda. Notice that you invite the monitor to speak after you. You are not hiding his report. You are making sure the room hears your framing first and his as confirmation.

The lines to say

Say the number in dollars, not as a percentage: "about 1,200,000 dollars over" lands as honest, while "a modest variance" lands as spin. Say the method: "This is budget divided by the cost index, assuming the rest of the job runs at today's efficiency." Say what you control: "Of the 1,200,000 dollars, about 700,000 is ground and already spent. The other 500,000 is a forecast we can still influence." Say the plan with dates: "Revised mechanical and finishes buyout by month 8; value-engineering options priced by the 15th; my equity deposit plan, if one is needed, by Friday."

Say that out loud now.

The number, the range, the cause, the plan. In dollars. Before anyone asks.

The lines never to say

Never say "We will make it up later." The lender has heard it on every project that went out of balance, and the to-complete index from Day 5, about 1.07, says it is unlikely. Never say "The contractor's numbers are wrong" with the contractor in the room unless you can prove it on the spot; it turns a cost review into a dispute in front of your lender. Never say "It is within contingency" if contingency is being consumed faster than work is completed. And never promise the lender a number you have not checked: "I will confirm by Friday" is stronger than a guess.

What to put on the table

Bring one page, printed, for each person. At the top, the forecast final cost and the range. Below it, the bridge from last month's forecast to this month's, one line per cause, in dollars. Then contingency remaining against work remaining, the earned value indices, and the actions with owners and dates. A single page signals that you know which numbers matter. A thick pack signals that you hope nobody finds the one that does.

The question behind the question

The relationship manager asks, "Is the loan still in balance?" The question behind it is, "Will I have to call this in to my credit committee, and will you fund the gap?" Answer both: "On the revised forecast, cost to complete exceeds undisbursed funds by about 400,000 dollars after remaining contingency. I will deposit that amount before the next draw, and you will have the deposit schedule in writing."

The monitor asks, "How did you measure percent complete on concrete?" The question behind it is, "Are you using billing or quantities?" Answer with the method and the evidence: "Placed and accepted cubic metres against design quantity, from the pour log, which I will send you today."

The contractor's manager says, "We can recover the schedule if we add a second crew." The question behind it may be, "Will you pay for acceleration?" Do not agree in the room. Say: "Send me the cost and time effect in writing, and we will decide on the record."

When to stay silent

Stay silent after you state the number. The temptation is to fill the silence with reassurance, and reassurance sounds like doubt. Let the lender ask the next question. Stay silent while the monitor gives his view, even where he differs; take notes, and respond to the difference in writing with evidence, not in the room with irritation.

Holding your state

A forecast overrun in front of your lender will raise your heart rate. That is normal and it is not a signal to talk faster. Before the meeting, while parked, take a few slow breaths with longer out-breaths than in-breaths; check that with your doctor if you have any heart or breathing condition. In the room, slow your speech at the number, look at the person you are addressing, and treat the meeting as an operations report rather than a judgement on you. You have run shift handovers where the bad news had to be stated plainly to the next operator; this is the same discipline.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is arriving with a report that disagrees with the monitor's, so that the meeting becomes a debate about whose number is right instead of a plan. The control is to reconcile your forecast with the monitor's draft, if the lender will share it, or with your own earned value from quantities, before you walk in.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner leads with explanations and arrives at the number last, so the room spends ten minutes wondering how bad it is. Lead with the number.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught the hostile-question pattern: acknowledge, bridge, answer. When the relationship manager says, "You told us three months ago this was on budget," acknowledge it: "I did, and that report was built on spending, not earned value." Bridge: "What has changed is how we measure." Answer: "Here is the forecast on quantities, and here is how you will receive it every month from now on."

Recap

Open with the forecast, the range, the cause and the plan, in dollars and before anyone asks. Answer the question behind each question, refuse to agree new costs in the room, and stay silent after the number. Reconcile with the monitor beforehand so the meeting is about the plan, not the arithmetic.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: six questions on cost control, a Red Pen drill on a monthly cost report, and the boardroom drill.
checklist: I reconcile my forecast with the monitor's method before the meeting.
I open with the forecast final cost, the range, the cause and the plan.
I state the overrun in dollars, with the forecasting method named.
I separate cost already incurred from cost I can still influence.
I answer the lender's balance question with a deposit amount and date.
I refuse to agree acceleration or other new costs in the room.
I stay silent after stating the number and let the lender ask next.
I commit to dates for every follow-up and confirm them in writing.
head: Field checklist
speak: In the monthly cost meeting I state the bad number first, because whoever states it owns the conversation. I open with four sentences: our forecast final cost is about 13,200,000 dollars against a 12,000,000 budget, the range is about 12,500,000 to 14,200,000, the cause is shallow rock in the foundations and a concrete package bought above estimate, and here is the plan. I say it in dollars, name the method, and separate cost already spent from cost I can still influence. When the lender asks whether the loan is in balance, I answer the question behind it: the shortfall, and when I will deposit it. When the monitor asks how I measured progress, I say quantities, not billing, and send the evidence. When the contractor offers acceleration, I ask for the cost and time effect in writing. And after I say the number, I stop talking.
terms: Lender's monitor — an independent engineer or cost consultant appointed by the lender to report on progress, cost and draw requests.
Bridge — a line-by-line reconciliation showing how a forecast moved from an earlier figure to the current one.
Acceleration — action to finish work faster than the current schedule, such as extra crews or overtime, usually at extra cost.

hostile.q: You told us three months ago this project was on budget. Why should we trust today's forecast?
hostile.a: That report was built on spending against plan, and it should have been built on earned value. I own that. Today's forecast measures progress from verified quantities, it matches your monitor's method, and it shows a range rather than a single convenient number. From now on you will receive the same columns every month, with every line that moved explained in writing, so you can test it rather than trust it.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 51 Review: Layers, Buyout, Earned Value and the Honest Forecast
summary: Six questions test the week's core ideas on construction cost: budget layers, buyout variance, Rule 51, the equity effect of an overrun, earned value and fixed-price risk. A Red Pen drill on a hypothetical monthly cost report, then a two-minute boardroom drill.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: a budget is a forecast you rebuild every month from commitments and measured progress, and you report it, in the dollars you will actually pay, before anyone else does.

Recall

Q. On the week's numbers, what was the yield on cost before and after the overrun?

A. About 7.0 percent at 20,000,000 dollars of cost, falling to about 6.36 percent at 22,000,000 dollars, against a 5.5 percent market cap rate.

Q. What does an exclusion in a scope document do?

A. It states work that is not in the contractor's price. Every exclusion must be bought by someone else or accepted as a gap, or it becomes a change order later.

Q. What is a break-even in a stress test?

A. The value of one input, such as rent, cost or exit cap rate, at which a chosen measure just reaches its limit, for example the point where equity returns fall to zero or the loan's coverage test fails.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, cost is where every promise in your pro forma is either kept or broken. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you can run a cost meeting with a lender, a monitor and a contractor and remain the person in the room who knows the number first. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What are the layers of a construction budget, and why keep them on separate lines?

Answer: Base estimate, allowances, escalation and contingency, with contingency itself split into design contingency, the owner's construction contingency and sometimes a contractor's contingency. Kept apart, you can see each one move; merged, escalation and allowances quietly make contingency look larger than it is.

Question 2. What is buyout variance, and what do you do with a favourable one?

Answer: The difference between a package's estimate and its awarded price. A favourable variance is information, not profit: hold it as protection for packages not yet bought until the remaining risk is small.

Question 3. State Rule 51.

Answer: Report the forecast final cost, in the dollars you will actually pay, every month to the people funding the project, and never let a published estimate leave out a cost you know you will pay.

Question 4. Why does a 10 percent overrun cut equity profit by far more than 10 percent?

Answer: Because the loan is usually fixed at closing, so the whole overrun is paid with equity. On the week's hypothetical numbers, profit fell 37 percent and the equity multiple fell from about 1.78 to about 1.38 times.

Question 5. Give the formulas for the cost performance index and the most common estimate at completion.

Answer: Cost performance index is earned value divided by actual cost. The common estimate at completion is budget at completion divided by the cost performance index, which assumes the rest of the job runs at today's efficiency.

Question 6. Under a fixed price, why has price risk not really disappeared?

Answer: Because the contractor priced it into the bid, and if prices rise beyond what it can absorb, it may fail, slow down or pursue claims, and the risk returns to the owner.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Quincy layered the budget and introduced bid packages, buyout variance and earned value. Ford and Roman took Boston's Central Artery project, where the estimate drifted away from the truth and trust collapsed with it, giving Rule 51. Nadia showed how a 10 percent overrun becomes a 37 percent profit problem for the equity, and how escalation compounds to each package's midpoint. LEX showed how fixed price, cost reimbursement and index clauses allocate rising prices, and compared Canada and Guyana. The Red Pen

Read this hypothetical monthly cost report summary. Find the defects before reading on.

Monthly Cost Report, Month 7. Original budget 12,000,000 dollars. Spent to date 6,100,000 dollars against planned spend of 6,300,000 dollars: project 200,000 dollars under budget. Percent complete 55 percent, per contractor's payment application. Contingency 1,200,000 dollars, unchanged since design development, including escalation and the finishes allowance. Concrete package awarded 150,000 dollars over estimate; we expect to recover this on later packages. Forecast final cost: 12,000,000 dollars. Escalation: nil, all prices at estimate date. Prepared by: Contractor's quantity surveyor.

The defects. First, "under budget" compares spending with planned spending and says nothing about work done; without earned value the claim is meaningless and may be the opposite of the truth. Second, percent complete comes from the contractor's payment application, so it measures billing, not verified quantities. Third, contingency is unchanged since design development, which is implausible after buyout has begun, and it includes escalation and an allowance, so it is overstated. Fourth, the concrete overrun is assumed to be recovered later: hope, not a forecast. Fifth, the forecast final cost equals the original budget, which means it was copied, not forecast, and it ignores the known concrete variance. Sixth, escalation is nil with all prices at the estimate date, breaching Rule 51 by leaving out a cost that will certainly be paid. Seventh, the report is prepared by the contractor's quantity surveyor; the owner's forecast must come from someone who reports to the owner.

Then the corrected version: earned value from quantities, contingency separated from escalation and allowances, buyout variance recorded and carried into the forecast, escalation to each package's midpoint, a forecast final cost with a range, and the owner's cost consultant's name at the bottom.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to an investor who asks, "How do you know this project will come in on budget?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "I do not know it will, and anyone who says they know is guessing. What I do is forecast the final cost every month from what we have actually bought and the work actually done. The budget is in layers: base estimate, allowances, escalation and contingency, each on its own line so none can hide another. Every package we award shows whether the estimate held. We measure progress from quantities, not the contractor's bills, and compare it with what was planned and what was spent, so we see a cost problem at month 6, not month 11. The forecast is stated in the dollars we will actually pay, including escalation and pending changes, and it is checked by a cost consultant who reports to me. If it moves, you hear it from me first, with the cause, the range and the plan. And remember, because the loan is fixed, an overrun lands on our equity, so I protect contingency until the last package is bought."

Score your own answer before comparing. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you name the budget layers and the earned value idea? Did you state Rule 51? Did you finish inside two minutes? If you missed any, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a cost report that looks precise and measures the wrong thing: spending instead of earned value, billing instead of quantities, budget remaining instead of forecast. The control is a fixed format every month, built by your own cost consultant, with the forecast method stated.

The beginner's mistake

Memorising the earned value formulas without insisting on how earned value is measured. The formulas are easy. The measurement decides whether they tell the truth.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman taught that a severe case is not a pessimist's fantasy but a planned response. The three estimates at completion from Day 5 are exactly that applied to cost: an optimistic, a base and a severe forecast, each with its assumption, so that the response to the severe one is planned before it arrives.

Recap

Layer the budget, record buyout, measure earned value from quantities, forecast from commitments, escalate to each package's midpoint, and report the forecast final cost monthly in the dollars you will pay. Rule 51 holds it together.

head: The six questions
speak: Construction cost is controlled by an honest forecast, not by the budget I approved at the start. I keep the budget in layers: base estimate, allowances, escalation and contingency, each on its own line. Every bid package awarded shows a buyout variance, and a favourable one is protection, not profit. I measure progress as earned value, from verified quantities, and compare it with planned value and actual cost. Earned value over actual cost is the cost index; budget divided by that index is my usual forecast final cost, shown with a range. Because the loan is fixed at closing, an overrun lands on my equity, so a 10 percent cost problem can be a 37 percent profit problem. A fixed price moves price risk to the contractor on paper, at a premium, and it can come back if the contractor cannot carry it. Rule 51: report the forecast final cost, in the dollars I will actually pay, every month, and never leave out a cost I know I will pay.
terms: Forecast method — the stated assumption behind an estimate at completion, such as remaining work at budget or at today's cost efficiency.
Percent complete — the share of a cost line's work that is done, which must be measured from verified quantities or agreed milestones.
Owner's cost consultant — a quantity surveyor or cost consultant engaged by and reporting to the owner, independent of the design and construction teams.

hostile.q: Your cost report says forecast final cost equals the original budget, at month 7, with a package already bought over estimate. Is anyone actually forecasting?
hostile.a: On that report, no, and I withdraw it. A forecast equal to the original budget after a known overrun was copied, not forecast. You will have a replacement within a set number of days, prepared by my own cost consultant: earned value from quantities, the concrete variance carried in, escalation to each package's midpoint, contingency separated from allowances and escalation, and a forecast final cost with its method and range.
